title: Places and journeys
job: A trip told in full, with directions inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: V-(eu)n jeok isseoyo IS THE EXPERIENCE PAST — it is among the things I have done. gasseoyo says I went, on a particular day. Korean keeps the two strictly apart where English folds them into have been.
THE DIRECTION LIVES INSIDE THE VERB: deureogayo goes in, nagayo goes out, ollagayo goes up, naeryeogayo goes down, doragayo goes back. English hangs a preposition on go; Korean builds a new verb.
-e IS THE DESTINATION REACHED, -(eu)ro THE DIRECTION FACED. English to is both. San-e gayo arrives at the mountain; oenjjok-euro gayo only heads left, and may never get anywhere.

L2-M4's DIRECTIONS ARE REUSED WHOLE and nothing is added to them: oenjjok, oreunjjok, jjuk, geonneoseyo, doraseyo, sageori, naeriseyo, taseyo. A journey that needs a word L2-M4 has not got is the wrong journey.
A TRIP IS TOLD WITH L2-M10's SEQUENCERS — meonjeo, geu daeum-e, machimnae — and the directions live INSIDE the telling rather than in a list. That is the whole skill this module adds.
gaseo IS L2-M10's AND CHAINS ARRIVING TO DOING: you go, and then, being there, you do the next thing. -go would only list two acts and would lose the being there.

AN ENGLISH SPEAKER'S KOREAN TRIP COMES OUT PREPOSITION-HEAVY AND VERB-LIGHT — up the mountain, out of the station, back to the house. Every one of those is a single Korean verb, and reaching for wi, bakk or arae rebuilds the English.
chulbal AND dochak ARE L4-M7's, borrowed here for a timetable and nothing else. The announcement register itself stays behind at M7.

sentences.cue: Have you ever been to the sea?

words.note: Both the sea and the beach you go to. bada-e gayo is what a Korean says for a trip to the coast, with no separate word for the shore.
gada plus L4-M1's trial auxiliary, joined, then the past modifier. It is the fixed shape of this frame; ga bwasseoyo would put L2-M10's seeing into a sentence about going.
A bound noun that counts occasions, so it needs a modifier in front and isseoyo or eopseoyo after. On its own it is not a word.

sentences.trap: This asks whether it is on your list at all, not when you went. Answering with a date answers a question that was not asked.
sentences.sound: BA-da-e GA-bon JEOK I-sseo-yo? The question rises only at the very end.

variations.cue: Have you ever been to the mountains?
variations.changed: a different place

variations.cue: Have you ever been to the airport?
variations.changed: somewhere ordinary, where the frame still works

mistake.why: Split into two words, bwasseoyo is L2-M10's saw, and the sentence turns into something about looking. The experience frame is gabon jeok isseoyo, written as it is.

sentences.usage: Small talk with somebody you have just met.

sentences.cue: I went on a trip and saw the sea.

words.note: Takes gada rather than hada in the ordinary phrase: yeohaeng-eul gayo, to go on a trip.

sentences.trap: gaseo is not and then in general. It says that the second thing happened THERE, once you had arrived, which is why a trip is told with it.

variations.cue: I went on a trip and saw the mountains.
variations.changed: what was seen there

variations.cue: The trip was really good.
variations.changed: the trip as the subject, closing an account

mistake.why: -go lists two separate acts and loses the connection: it could be read as going on a trip, and separately seeing the sea. gaseo ties the second to the place the first reached.

sentences.mnemonic: gaseo means go and then, right there.

sentences.display: San-e gabon jeok isseoyo. Eoje-neun an gasseoyo.
sentences.script: 산에 가본 적 있어요. 어제는 안 갔어요.
sentences.cue: I have been to the mountains before. I did not go yesterday.
sentences.literal: mountain-to gone-tried-MODIFIER instance exist. yesterday-TOP not went

words.note: Korea's default weekend outing, so the word turns up far more often than the English mountain does.

sentences.trap: Both halves are about the same place, and they are not the same tense in meaning. The first says it is among my experiences; the second reports one particular day.
sentences.sound: SA-ne GA-bon JEOK I-sseo-yo. EO-je-neun AN GA-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: I went to the mountains.
variations.changed: the plain past on its own — one occasion, no claim about experience

variations.cue: I have never been to the sea.
variations.changed: the negative of the frame, which uses eopseoyo

mistake.why: jeok takes the plain -(eu)n modifier, and the trial auxiliary is what carries the having-tried. Stacking a past on the modifier is a shape Korean does not build.

sentences.usage: Correcting somebody who assumed you were there yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: Ever is a frame; yesterday is a tense.

sentences.cue: Turn back to the left at the crossroads.

words.note: dolda plus gada, joined into one verb: the turning and the going are a single word. L2-M4's doraseyo only turns; this one turns and leaves.

sentences.trap: -(eu)ro is the direction faced, so oenjjok-euro is off to the left. oenjjok-e would name a place on the left and stop the sentence going anywhere.

variations.cue: Turn back to the right at the crossroads.
variations.changed: the other side

variations.cue: I turn back to the left at the bus stop.
variations.changed: your own account rather than an instruction

mistake.why: -e puts you AT the left, which a turn cannot do. Movement toward something takes -(eu)ro, and this is the particle pair English to hides.

sentences.usage: Directions given on a street corner.

sentences.cue: I went into the airport and met my friend.

words.note: Airport. The ng at the end of the first syllable is held, which is what keeps it apart from gohang.
deulda plus gada. The in is already inside the verb, so nothing else in the sentence has to say it.

sentences.trap: There is no word here for into. Adding one is the English sentence rebuilt on Korean words, and it is what makes a learner's directions sound translated.

variations.cue: I go into the house and rest.
variations.changed: the everyday use — going indoors

variations.cue: I went to the airport and met my friend.
variations.changed: plain gaseo, which says nothing about going inside

mistake.why: Two words doing one verb's job. Korean has deureogada for exactly this, and spelling the in out separately is the preposition habit English brings.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how a meeting happened.
sentences.mnemonic: The direction is in the verb.

sentences.cue: You go out of the station and take a taxi.

words.note: The mirror of deureogayo, built the same way from nada and gada. -eseo on the station is the from that goes with it.

sentences.trap: -eseo marks where the leaving starts. yeok-e nagayo would say going out TO the station, which is the wrong end of the journey.

variations.cue: Go out of the station and head left.
variations.changed: an instruction rather than a description

variations.cue: I go out of the house.
variations.changed: the verb on its own, with nothing after it

mistake.why: Again two words for one verb. nagada already means to go out, and bakk-euro gada is the English out of translated piece by piece.

sentences.usage: The middle of a set of directions.
sentences.mnemonic: In is deureo-, out is na-.

sentences.display: San-e ollagal ttae sigan-i mani geollyeosseoyo.
sentences.script: 산에 올라갈 때 시간이 많이 걸렸어요.
sentences.cue: It took a long time going up the mountain.
sentences.literal: mountain-to go-up-MODIFIER time time-SUBJ a-lot took

words.note: oreuda plus gada, with the r doubling into ll. Before L4-M6's ttae it takes the -l modifier: ollagal ttae.

sentences.trap: geollyeosseoyo is L3-M7's and takes sigan as its subject, not you. Korean says the time took itself; there is no I in the sentence at all.
sentences.sound: SA-ne OL-la-gal TTAE SI-ga-ni MA-ni GEOL-lyeo-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: I go up the mountain.
variations.changed: the bare verb

variations.cue: It took time going up the mountain.
variations.changed: without mani, so no judgement about how long

mistake.display: San-e wi-ro gal ttae sigan-i mani geollyeosseoyo.
mistake.script: 산에 위로 갈 때 시간이 많이 걸렸어요.
mistake.why: wi-ro gada is up the way English says it. Korean has ollagada, and using the preposition shape here is the interference this module is built around.

sentences.cue: I got lost on the way down.

words.note: naerida plus gada. L2-M4's naeriseyo gets off a bus; this one carries on down a road, and the two are not interchangeable.
Both the road itself and the way to somewhere. gil-eul ireobeoryeosseoyo, to lose the way, is the fixed phrase for getting lost.

sentences.trap: Korean loses the ROAD, not itself. There is no I got lost with you as the object; the thing mislaid is the way.

variations.cue: The way down is long.
variations.changed: the road as subject

variations.cue: I go down the mountain.
variations.changed: the mountain as the path travelled, which takes -eul

mistake.why: arae-ro gada is down built the English way. The single verb naeryeogada is what Korean uses, and it is the whole point of the set.

sentences.usage: The part of the story where it went wrong.

sentences.cue: I looked at the map and went straight on to the right.

words.note: A map, on paper or on a phone. It goes with bogo, to look at, rather than with a verb of reading.

sentences.trap: bogo, not bogoseo. L3-M6's -go simply stacks the two acts here; the map is not a place you arrive at, so gaseo's being-there is not wanted.
sentences.sound: JI-do-reul BO-go O-reun-jjo-geu-ro JJUK GA-sseo-yo. jjuk is one short tense burst.

variations.cue: I looked at the map and went left.
variations.changed: the other side, and no jjuk

variations.cue: I have a map.
variations.changed: the map as subject

mistake.why: jjuk is a straight run in a direction, so the particle has to be -(eu)ro. -e would fix a point, and you cannot run straight on at a point.

sentences.usage: Retelling how you found the place.

sentences.display: Meonjeo gonghang-e gasseoyo. Geu daeum-e bada-e gasseoyo. Machimnae jip-e doragasseoyo.
sentences.script: 먼저 공항에 갔어요. 그 다음에 바다에 갔어요. 마침내 집에 돌아갔어요.
sentences.cue: First I went to the airport. Then I went to the sea. Finally I went back home.
sentences.literal: first airport-to went. that next-at sea-to went. finally house-to went-back

words.note: The past of S04's doragayo, and the ordinary way an account of a trip ends. Going back is one verb, not a verb plus back.

sentences.trap: The sequencers are L2-M10's and carry the whole shape of the account. Nothing new is needed to tell a trip; what is new is putting the directions inside it.
sentences.sound: MEON-jeo GONG-hang-e GA-sseo-yo. GEU DA-eu-me BA-da-e GA-sseo-yo. MA-chim-nae JI-be DO-ra-ga-sseo-yo.

variations.display: Meonjeo yeok-e gasseoyo. Geu daeum-e bada-e gasseoyo. Machimnae jip-e doragasseoyo.
variations.script: 먼저 역에 갔어요. 그 다음에 바다에 갔어요. 마침내 집에 돌아갔어요.
variations.cue: First I went to the station. Then to the sea. Finally I went back home.
variations.changed: where the trip starts

variations.cue: Finally I went back home.
variations.changed: the closing line alone

mistake.display: Meonjeo gonghang-e gabon jeok isseoyo. Geu daeum-e bada-e gasseoyo.
mistake.script: 먼저 공항에 가본 적 있어요. 그 다음에 바다에 갔어요.
mistake.why: The experience frame cannot sit inside a chronological account: it says at some point in my life, which meonjeo immediately contradicts. Inside a trip, every step is a plain past.

sentences.usage: Telling the whole of a day out.
sentences.mnemonic: A trip is plain pasts on a string.

comprehensionPool.cue: Have you ever been to the sea?
I have never been to the mountains.
I went on a trip and saw the sea.
Turn back to the left at the crossroads.
I went into the airport and met my friend.
You go out of the station and take a taxi.

comprehensionPool.display: San-e ollagal ttae sigan-i mani geollyeosseoyo.
comprehensionPool.script: 산에 올라갈 때 시간이 많이 걸렸어요.
comprehensionPool.cue: It took a long time going up the mountain.
I got lost on the way down.
I looked at the map and went straight on to the right.
It took an hour from station to station.
